transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Georgia Democratic Senator John Ossoff
has won a second term after his aggressive campaign
against President Trump's pick for the seat,
Republican Congressman Mike Collins.
That's according to a race call from the Associated Press.
Ossoff has raised more than $80 million.
That's the most of any Senate nominee this year.
It's helped him go from being widely considered
as Democrats most vulnerable in comment to being mentioned
as a potential 2028 presidential contender.
Voters are deciding control of the U.S. House and Senate.
NPR's White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben
is with me in the studio. Hi, Danielle.
Hey there.
So Republicans are defending seats in some states
where President Trump won.
This is a very different environment to what they had anticipated.
How did we get here?
Well, President Trump definitely looms over all of this.
I mean, he's not only the leader of the party.
He reshaped the GOP, and now he's deeply unpopular.
Many polls put his approval rating below 40 percent,
which puts it in historic territory.
According to Gallup, George W. Bush in 2006
had the worst pre-election approval rating since 1946 at 37 percent.
So Trump's around there.
Now, the economy is a huge part of this.
We normally say the president doesn't get direct credit
or blame for the economy, but Trump,
with his unilateral decisions on tariffs,
his war with Iran, has affected prices.
And polls show that voters do blame him for that.
So this election has also given some Republicans
very little chance to try to run campaigns
that separate themselves from the president.
It seems like tonight will be a test of that strategy.
Absolutely.
And Trump has been telling crowds ahead of this election
to pretend he's on the ballot.
Now, that might help some.
His followers are loyal, so maybe he can drive some turnout.
But if you're a Republican in a battleground race
like Ohio, Iowa, Michigan, you probably want more voters
than just the loyal MAGA crowd.
And it's unclear that Trump can pull in those independent votes.
Now, one Republican who is not tying themselves to Trump
is Maine Susan Collins,
who is in the fight of her political life for her Senate seat.
She's run a race based on her independence
and her ability to bring dollars to the state.
And her race will likely be critical to controlling the Senate.
All right, NPR White House correspondent Danielle Kurtzleben,
thank you so much.
Thank you.
So next our polls will close in Iowa.
NPR's Stephen Fowler is there reporting on several competitive races.
Iowa is a state that wasn't on many people's radar
coming into this election cycle,
but it's an agriculture-heavy state
that's been affected heavily by Trump administration,
economic policies, tariffs, rising prices, you name it.
That's why there's a competitive race for governor,
U.S. Senate, and three of its four House seats that I'm watching
that will be on the front lines of determining
which party controls each chamber of Congress.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reporting.
Democrats are also hoping to take over a majority of governor's offices
for the first time in two decades.
The surprising number of states that are in play
is a sign of voter discontent
and Republican President Trump's poor approval ratings.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Latino civil rights group Unidos U.S. is criticizing ICE
for a social media post today that said in part,
"If you vote illegally, we will find you."
Latino turnout was expected to be high for the midterm elections.
That's why the message went out.
The Department of Homeland Security issued a statement saying,
"Only Americans should elect American leaders."
Throughout the day, ICE announced arrests or charges
against people suspected of voting as non-citizens in previous elections.
Around 25 million naturalized citizens are eligible to vote.
Even though naturalization ceremonies have slowed down
under the second Trump administration,
the number of new U.S. citizens has grown,
according to the Pew Research Center.
NPR's Sage Miller spoke to one new American voting
in his first general election.
Juan Escalante moved to the U.S. from Venezuela
when he was 11 years old.
He didn't know he was undocumented
until his junior year of high school.
He then spent more than two decades
navigating the immigration system.
Escalante doesn't have to do that anymore
because he became a U.S. citizen last year.
Now, at the age of 37,
he is voting in his very first general election in California.
Escalante says he was overwhelmed opening his ballot.
There were so many things to vote for.
You know, despite the amount of bubbles that I had to fill in
and the amount of research that I had to do,
I never once took that for granted as I was filling in my ballot.
Escalante says he is proud to be a U.S. citizen.
Sage Miller, NPR News.
A rebound for some influential big-tech stocks today
helped keep the U.S. market steady,
despite a fall for Apple and mixed trading elsewhere on Wall Street.
This is NPR News.
Pro today.

topics.text: Georgia Senator John Ossoff wins second term over Republican Mike Collins, per AP
NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben explains GOP challenges as Trump's unpopularity weighs on midterm races
Polls close in Iowa, where competitive governor, Senate, and House races are being watched
Democrats hope to win a majority of governor's offices for first time in two decades
Latino group Unidos U.S. criticizes ICE post warning 'If you vote illegally, we will find you'
ICE announces arrests and charges against suspected noncitizen voters in past elections
Juan Escalante, a naturalized citizen from Venezuela, casts first general election vote in California
Big-tech stocks rebound and keep U.S. market steady despite Apple's decline
